name: Sigari 2017, boat engravings at Boyuk Das
citation: Sigari, D. (2017). Portrayal of a sea in a semiarid environment: Boat engravings in Böyük Daş, Gobustan. Journal of Arid Environments 143, 57-63 (August 2017). DOI 10.1016/j.jaridenv.2016.12.012. ISSN 0140-1963. Elsevier, PII S0140196316302385. Received 18 January 2016, revised 23 August 2016, accepted 29 December 2016, available online 4 January 2017 (dates printed on p. 57). Copy read: the author's own upload on Academia.edu, https://www.academia.edu/30761555/Portrayal_of_a_sea_in_a_semiarid_environment_Boat_engravings_in_B%C3%B6y%C3%BCk_Da%C5%9F_Gobustan (page previews at https://attachments.academia-assets.com/53198700/1.html to 7.html). Repository records, metadata only: https://iris.unife.it/handle/11392/2482658 (University of Ferrara) and https://hal.science/hal-03806860 (HAL).
source_tier: Peer-reviewed journal article (Journal of Arid Environments, Elsevier). Single-author paper presenting a preliminary field study with a proposed relative chronology. The acknowledgments thank George Nash and Davida Eisenberg-Degen 'for the invitation', which suggests an invited contribution to a themed issue [uncertain: the special-issue title was not confirmed].
access_status: Fully read as text. The publisher version is paywalled (Unpaywall and OpenAlex both list it as closed; ScienceDirect returned an error to direct fetches). The Ferrara repository record given in the brief returned HTTP 403 to every direct request and, per OpenAlex and HAL, holds no full-text file. The openable copy is the author's Academia.edu upload: its seven page previews are the typeset journal pages (pp. 57-63) and were read in full on 10 October 2026, including abstract, all five sections, figure captions, acknowledgments and references. Figures were read through captions only; the images were not inspected. The PDF download itself needs an Academia.edu account and was not used.
author_credentials: Dario Sigari, rock art archaeologist. Affiliation on the paper: Università degli Studi di Ferrara, Dipartimento di Studi Umanistici. ORCID 0000-0002-7427-0877 (from Crossref). Fieldwork at Gobustan: yes. The paper reports 'a fieldwork carried out in July 2015' and thanks Gobustan Reserve staff (Kamran Abbassov, Sevinc Shirinli, Rehman Abdullayev) and the former director Malahat Farajova. He had published on Rock 44 of Böyük Daş in 2013 and later led the 2019-2024 project at Ana Zaga reported in Sigari et al. 2025. The paper states its limits: he 'did not have the possibility to access and document other rocks still considered unpublished' and filled gaps with tracings by Djafarsade, Rustamov and Farajova.

exact_quotes.quote: From a stylistic point of view informed by preliminary studies, it seems that boat figures have been engraved over a long span of time, suggesting the importance of the aquatic environment of the past.

However, in both cases the entire archaeological context has not yet been cleared nor published but, only their depth and the depth of the dated sample (see Farajova, 2012: 937), hence, its reliability cannot be taken into account in order to purpose an interpretation of the archaeological datum.

forgetting that he edited a tracing of Rock No. 29 where a boat, attributed to the I/E phase, is underimposed by an aurochs of the Phase II/B (Anati, 2001, 30). Therefore, because of this non clearness, Anati's work will be taken into account only as a first step to order the palimpsest, but it is critically accepted.

Up to now, the Early Khvalynian transgression period of the Caspian Sea seems to be the one that has mostly characterised the landscape in Gobustan possibly during the first peopling of the region, when the two hills of Böyük Daş and Kiçik Daş appeared as two islands.
Moreover on the different terraces there are rocks with a characteristic hole, probably used to dock the boats.

Nine rocks with boat figures have been recorded, both on upper (labelled as Rock No. 29, 30, 765A, 41, 42 and two small unnumbered rocks, considered together as [unnumbered], on either side of the stairs leading to the Öküzlər cave) and lower (Rock No. 8) terraces of the mountain of Böyük Daş, and one (Rock No. 19) from Kiçik Daş.
Accompanying these ships are sun-like symbols that can be set at the end of the prow line or can be realised by curving the prow and adding the rays.

During the preliminary fieldwork, the height of the engravings from the soil-line was taken into account, even though it may be difficult to obtain samples for understanding the chronology of each panel.
Rock No. 29 is a large boulder that is set on the upper terrace of Böyük Daş. It forms the southern side of Ana Zaga cave. The boulder is probably in its original position.

Rock No. 29 is engraved on three of its surfaces: the southern, eastern and northern surfaces. Boat figures are present on both southern and northern faces and are associated, over/underimposed and juxtaposed with anthropomorphic and zoomorphic figures.

Boat figure on the southern face of Rock No. 29 (Fig. 2) was realised using the natural shape of the rock that has a curved crack in its upper part, which suggested, to the artist, the keel of the boat. The prow is oriented eastwards, towards the Caspian Sea, and is decorated with a sun-shaped symbol. Concerning its relationship with the other figures, the boat overlaps both a zoomorph and two male anthropomorphs.
Differently from Anati's it is possible stating that the boat is more ancient than the aurochs, attributed to the phase II/B.
However, these three boats may appear slightly more recent than the one on southern surface that may belong to a previous phase.
Boat engraving on southern surface of Rock No. 29, Böyük Daş, upper terrace. The engraving is partially eroded by the toothpaste used to enlighten the figure.

we can suggest that the first boat images, which are set on the upper terraces of both Böyük Daş and Kiçik Daş, date back to a period of deglaciation, occurred between 16 and 14ka or even before. Then, from 14 to 12 ka cal. BP, the Later Khvalynian stages occurred, rising sea level between 0 and -12 m asl. To this period, or to a later one, can be dated the boat figures engraved on Rock No.8. Thus the new boat styles developed, spreading up to the upper terraces too, introducing new symbols like the sun one and the "X"-shaped crew.

To conclude, ship figures define a new space, a new scape into which stories are told. Although these stories can never be deciphered, the rock art narrative involves the importance of the Caspian Sea during prehistoric times

It is the view of the author that there is still much fieldwork and interpretative research to be done. A review of the rock art heritage, combined with sub-surface investigations and excavations is urgently required in order to better understand this enigmatic assemblage

key_claims: Boats are among the most recurrent themes at Gobustan and were engraved 'over a long span of time', changing style 'possibly according to new ideologies'. The paper calls its own basis 'preliminary studies'.

Corpus studied: nine rocks with boats. Eight on Böyük Daş (upper terrace: Rocks 29, 30, 765A, 41, 42 and two small unnumbered rocks treated as one; lower terrace: Rock 8) and one on Kiçik Daş (Rock 19). Fieldwork July 2015. This is a sample, not a census of Gobustan boats: the author says he could not reach unpublished rocks.

Boat typology. Long boats over 1.50 m on Rocks 29, 30, 765A and 41; shorter boats on Rocks 42, 8 and the unnumbered pair. Keels flat (Rock 29 north face east section, Rock 41) or curved (Rock 8). Crew shown as small vertical strokes (Rocks 29, 30, 765A, 41, 42) or as X-shaped elements (unnumbered rocks, Rock 8). Prows hooked; sun-like symbols at the end of the prow line or made by curving the prow and adding rays. Natural cracks in the rock are sometimes used as part of the boat (Rocks 29, 8, unnumbered).
Rock 29 is on the upper terrace of Böyük Daş, forms the southern side of Ana Zaga cave (the cave is made by Rocks 29, 30 and 31 set against each other) and is 'probably in its original position'.

Rock 29 south face: one boat, built on a natural curved crack that serves as the keel, prow pointing east towards the Caspian with a sun-shaped symbol. It overlaps a zoomorph and two male anthropomorphs, so on this panel the boat was cut after those figures.

Rock 29 north face: a long boat about 1.60 m in the eastern section, and three boats in three rows in the western section, all using natural curved fractures. The long boat is overlain by several mainly anthropomorphic figures and is older than the aurochs that Anati assigned to phase II/B.

The three western boats on the north face are overlain by a stylised male anthropomorph with a thin body and S-shaped legs that Anati put in a Holocene horizon (Phase III or IV), so the boats are older than that figure. They 'may appear slightly more recent than the one on southern surface'.
Three rocks are singled out as palimpsests that can order the boats: Rock 29, Rock 8 and Rock 19.

Rock 8 (lower terrace, current altitude 0 m asl): Djafarsade recorded 24 boats and eight female silhouettes. Boats are more curved, with sun symbols and hooked profiles, and recur beside aurochs. Female figures sit close to boats but never overlap them; male figures can lie under boats.

Rock 19, Kiçik Daş (20 to 30 m asl; the 'Firuz' site): around 34 boats in different styles, the number uncertain because the palimpsest is hard to read. Three have a sun-shaped prow and one an X-shaped crew.

Proposed relative chronology: the first boat images are those on the upper terraces of both hills, dated to the deglaciation of 16 to 14 ka 'or even before'. The boats on Rock 8 date to 14 to 12 ka cal. BP 'or to a later one'. New styles then developed and spread back up to the upper terraces, bringing the sun symbol and the X-shaped crew.

Earlier chronologies are treated as unreliable. Anati's is used only as a starting point because his own tracing of Rock 29 contradicts his phase order. The published radiocarbon dates from the deposits are set aside because their context is unpublished.
Holes in rocks on the terraces were 'probably used to dock the boats'. The terraces are 'possibly' ancient beaches.
The paper says the stories told by the boat figures 'can never be deciphered'.
evidence_offered: The author's own July 2015 field recording of nine rocks: 3D photogrammetry on Böyük Daş, photographs plus existing and new tracings for Rock 19. Tracings were drawn on photographs. Unreached rocks are covered from published tracings (Djafarsade 1973, Rustamov 2006, Farajova 2009, 2011, 2012). The chronology rests on three things: differences in boat style, the altitude and terrace of each rock, and which figure lies over which. These are then matched to a Caspian sea-level curve taken from other authors (chiefly Arslanov et al. 2015, with Levchenko and Roslyakov 2010 for the roughly 50 m maximum). Counts for Rock 8 (24 boats, eight female figures) come from Djafarsade and for Rock 19 (34 boats) from Farajova 2011. No new dates, no excavation, no sampling. No total count of boats on Rock 29 or across Böyük Daş is given.

motif_dates: First boat images, on the upper terraces of Böyük Daş and Kiçik Daş (the group Rock 29 belongs to): 'between 16 and 14ka or even before'. Worded as 'we can suggest'.
Boats on Rock 8, lower terrace: 14 to 12 ka cal. BP 'or to a later one'. No upper limit is stated.

Sun symbol and X-shaped crew: no absolute date. They are 'new symbols' that appear with the Rock 8 styles and then spread to the upper terraces, so by this scheme they are no earlier than about 14 to 12 ka and possibly later.
Rock 29 north face, long boat (about 1.60 m): 'a very ancient chronology'; older than the aurochs of Anati's phase II/B. No absolute date for this boat is given.
Rock 29 north face, three western boats: older than a male figure of Anati's Holocene Phase III or IV.
Rock 29 south face, sun-prow boat: no absolute date. Later than the zoomorph and two male figures it overlaps, and said to be possibly earlier than the three western boats on the north face.
Farajova's scheme, as reported: most ship images fall in the 4th style of her 1st phase, which covers the Upper Palaeolithic and Mesolithic.
Nowhere does the paper assign a boat to the Bronze Age. The word 'Bronze' does not occur in it.
site_and_layer_dates: First occupation of Gobustan 20,000 to 17,000 years ago (Rustamov 2006).

Ana Zaga deposit sample from bones, soil and ash at 1.85 m: 8996 ± 33 BP (Farajova 2012: 937). The paper prints this as 'BP cal.' [uncertain whether the figure is calibrated; Sigari et al. 2025 give it as plain BP].
A second sample 'of some 14.000 years ago', presented at the XIX IFRAO Congress in Cáceres, without published context.

Firuz site at Rock 19: finds from Upper Palaeolithic to Copper Age; a burial of one child and ten adults attributed to 10,000 years ago, with objects read as tools for knotting fishing nets (Rustamov 2006).
Archaeological finds across the reserve run 'from the Upper Palaeolithic to the Middle Age'. This is the occupation span, not a span for the boats.

Caspian levels (after Arslanov et al. 2015): Early Khvalynian maximum +48 to +50 m asl; transgressions to +35 and +22 m at about 16 to 14 ka cal. BP; two more at 14 to 12 ka cal. BP reaching 0 and -12 m asl. Total late Pleistocene amplitude 120 to 150 m.

dating_method: Relative only. Style, superimposition on palimpsest panels, and altitude of the rock matched to Caspian shorelines dated by other researchers (14C and 230Th/234U on Khvalynian deposits, Arslanov et al. 2015). The logic for the lower terrace is a terminus post quem: a rock at 0 m asl cannot have been carved while under water. The paper takes no samples and dates no engraving directly. It rejects the two radiocarbon dates from the deposits as a basis for interpretation because the archaeological context is unpublished, and notes that it 'may be difficult to obtain samples' for any panel. It also admits the Caspian chronology itself 'is still ongoing' as a debate.
panel_details: Rock No. 29, Böyük Daş, upper terrace; forms the southern side of Ana Zaga cave, which is made by Rocks 29, 30 and 31 set together. Judged 'probably in its original position' on three grounds: all engravings share one orientation, figures run below the soil on both south and north sides, and the south face is partly covered by another boulder. Engraved on three surfaces: south, east and north. South face (Fig. 2): one boat using a natural curved crack as its keel, prow to the east towards the Caspian, sun-shaped symbol on the prow; it overlaps one zoomorph and two male anthropomorphs. The engraving is partly eroded by toothpaste that earlier researchers used to highlight it. North face, eastern section (Fig. 3): one long boat about 1.60 m, flat keel, crew as short vertical strokes; juxtaposed with, over and under other figures; overlain by several mainly anthropomorphic figures; older than an aurochs. North face, western section: three boats in three rows on natural curved fractures, possibly enhanced by blue clay in the rock; the central boat is overlain by a thin-bodied male figure with S-shaped legs; surface heavily eroded. That makes five boats described on Rock 29 (one south, four north). The paper does not say this is the full count. The east face is engraved but its content is not described. The paper does not mention wavy lines, water marks, armed figures, warriors or hunters on Rock 29.
geographic_claims: The Caspian Sea only. Gobustan is placed on the west shore of the Caspian, 60 km south of Baku, at the eastern end of the Greater Caucasus. At the Early Khvalynian high stand Böyük Daş and Kiçik Daş 'appeared as two islands', and their terraces are 'possibly' old beaches where the first inhabitants landed. The prow of the south-face boat on Rock 29 points east 'towards the Caspian Sea'. No river, route or destination is named. The Black Sea appears only in the title of a cited paper on flood hypotheses. There is no mention of the Kura, the Phasis, Colchis, Greece, Scandinavia, Jason or the Argonauts.
counter_evidence: Against a Bronze Age date for the Rock 29 boats: the only specialist study of this boat corpus puts the upper-terrace boats in the late Pleistocene (16 to 14 ka or earlier) and never mentions the Bronze Age.

The scheme does leave a gap that a later date could use. The sun-prow type is given no absolute date, and the Rock 8 window is '14 to 12 ka cal. BP ... or to a later one' with no ceiling. The paper does not rule out a much later sun-prow boat; it simply offers no evidence for one.

Against treating boat and human figures on the south face as one scene: the boat overlaps the two male figures and the zoomorph. It was cut across them afterwards. The paper describes the relation as superimposition, not as a composition.
Against any narrative reading: the author's own conclusion is that the stories 'can never be deciphered'.

Against firm dates of any kind: the chronology is called preliminary, is phrased as 'we can suggest', depends on a sea-level curve the paper says is still debated, and has no directly dated engraving behind it.

Internal tension over the south-face boat. It carries the sun symbol, which the conclusion treats as a late introduction to the upper terrace, yet section 4 says it 'may belong to a previous phase' relative to the three western boats on the north face. The paper does not resolve this.
Internal inconsistency on Rock 8: sun symbols are placed 'above the sterns' there, while the general typology and the Rock 29 description put the sun on the prow.
The sample is small (nine rocks) and partly second-hand, built on older tracings whose reliability the paper itself questions in Anati's case.

Disagreement with the 2025 team paper on one point: here the boulder covering part of the south face is evidence that Rock 29 has not moved; Sigari et al. 2025 describe Ana Zaga as 'displaced limestone boulders' and a slab fallen in a catastrophic event.
independent_corroboration: None found for the Argonaut proposal: this 2017 paper predates it and says nothing about Greek myth. For the paper's own chronology, corroboration is thin. Crossref lists 2 citing works and Semantic Scholar 3. The scheme is restated in Sigari 2020 and Sigari et al. 2025, both by the same lead author, so that is repetition and not an independent test. The sea-level stages are independent (Arslanov et al. 2015) but date the shorelines, not the carvings. [uncertain] The citing works by other authors were not identified or opened.
alternative_explanations: The paper's own reading is environmental and local: the boats record a long dependence of Gobustan communities on the Caspian, carved on or above former beaches, with fishing implied by net-making tools in the Firuz burial and by pierced mooring stones. Style change is put down to 'new ideologies', left unspecified. The sun symbol is described as a decorative feature and given no meaning. Competing chronologies are reported: Djafarsade's six styles in two phases; Anati's reordering into phases I/A to II/C, which places the Rock 29 boat later than the aurochs that actually overlies it; Rustamov's separate stylistic sequences for anthropomorphs, zoomorphs and boats; Farajova's six phases with most ships in the Upper Palaeolithic to Mesolithic first phase. The paper offers no ritual, funerary or solar-boat interpretation and does not discuss Scandinavian parallels.

Ligatures and split diacritics from the page rendering were restored (for example 'ﬁ gures' to 'figures', 'B oyük Das ¸' to 'Böyük Daş'); wording and the author's non-native phrasing ('purpose', 'enlighten', 'non clearness') are as printed.
Checked against the opened full text: Rock 29's position, the three grounds for its being in place, the three engraved faces, the south-face and north-face boats, and all superimposition statements.
Checked against the opened full text: the nine-rock corpus, rock numbers, terrace assignments, boat typology, Rock 8 and Rock 19 counts and altitudes.
Checked against the opened full text: the relative chronology and its hedges, and the Caspian sea-level figures as the paper reports them.
Checked against Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall and HAL APIs: journal, volume, pages, DOI, ISSN, publication month, ORCID, closed access status, and citation counts.

Checked by text search of the extracted paper: no occurrence of Bronze, Argonaut, Jason, Colchis, Kura, Heyerdahl, Scandinavia, myth, warrior, hunter or Neolithic. 'Black Sea' and 'wave' occur once each, both in titles of cited works.
Not checked: the University of Ferrara repository record (HTTP 403) and the ScienceDirect page. Their content is known only from search snippets and from the APIs above.
Not checked: the figures as images, so the described overlaps were not seen, only read.

Not checked: any of the works cited (Anati 2001, Arslanov et al. 2015, Farajova 2009-2012, Djafarsade 1973, Rustamov 2006, Levchenko and Roslyakov 2010). What they say is reported here only as Sigari summarises it.
Not checked: whether the extracted text matches the publisher PDF character for character. The copy read carries the journal's typeset layout, running heads and page numbers.
relevance_to_essay: This is the primary specialist description of Rock 29 and the only paper that sets out why the boats are dated as they are. It gives the essay three firm points. The south-face boat with the sun prow is real, is described in print, and points east to the Caspian. It is cut across two male figures and an animal, so the panel records at least two episodes of carving and cannot be assumed to be a single scene of a ship and its crew. And the dating is a hedged relative scheme tied to shorelines of 16 to 12 thousand years ago, with no directly dated carving and no Bronze Age phase. The paper also leaves the sun-prow type without an absolute date and says the meaning of the boats cannot be recovered, which is the honest limit on any origin-of-a-myth claim in either direction.
open_questions: Whether the south-face sun-prow boat is the one the Ragazas article uses, and whether that article's 'armed figures' are the two male anthropomorphs the boat overlaps.
The absolute age of the sun-prow style. This paper gives a floor (about 14 to 12 ka) and no ceiling.
Why the south-face boat is called possibly earlier than the north-face western boats when it carries a symbol the conclusion treats as late.
How many boats Rock 29 carries in total, and what is on its east face.
Whether Rock 29 is in its original position (this paper) or displaced (Sigari et al. 2025), which matters for any argument from its orientation.
Whether the boulder covering part of the south face can be dated to give a minimum age for the figures beneath it.
Which themed issue of the Journal of Arid Environments the paper belongs to, and who the citing authors are.
Whether the 8996 ± 33 BP date is calibrated.
